newsitem.title: BELGIUM: YEAREND - Spin-washed badgers and other New Year weirdness.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Spin-washed badgers and other New Year weirdness.

text.p: Crack the champagne at New Year for the badger in the rinse cycle, the man with the detonating nose and the itch that closed down a government.
Or raise a glass to the fumble-free condom, the chilli that foiled a rapist, and the boy whose parents named him Brfxxccxxmnp cccclllmmnprxvcl mnckssqlbb11116.
Not too squeamish? Then pop the bubbly for the lost finger that identified a carjacker, the world's largest gall stone, and the dog-skin coats that were all the rage in Mongolia.
It is time again to celebrate the weird, wonderful and sometimes disgusting stories that have graced the world's headlines over the past year.
Animals played their usual starring role, none more so than the badger that crawled into a British woman's washing machine and got an unexpected soak and spin.
Happily it survived the ordeal -- but only because the woman noticed her laundry was beginning to smell.
Two cats in Sweden managed to get their own back after their owner locked them in the bathroom. Somehow they turned on the taps and flooded the house. The bill came to $45,000.

Less lucky were the dogs in Mongolia that ended up as coats. But animal lovers can take heart from U.S. research showing that deer hunters risk heart attacks from all the excitement the bloodsport brings.
On the medical front, some kind of award must surely go to the American man who got an explosive charge stuck up his nose. One sneeze could have been fatal, but surgeons removed the object first.
A Colombian man had a 4.4 pound (2 kg) gall stone removed, a "boulder" which television displayed as proof. The man said he thought it would have been smaller.

It must have been quite a burden, but at least it has gone. One Swedish five-year old is stuck with a 38-letter and five number first name given to him by parents as "a pregnant, expressionistic devlopment that we see as an artistic creation."
Should you meet, Brfxxccxxmnp cccclllmmnprxvc lmnckssqlbb11116 is pronounced Albin.
Human invention, in the meantime, showed few limits as man worked hard to build a better condom.
A Monaco-based British designer came up with a fumble-free system. It has an applicator that reportedly allows lovers to maintain eye-contact while the condom is fitted.
In Vienna, an Austrian went one further, inventing a liquid condom that users paint on. One drawback is that it must be left for seven minutes to set. The manufacturer recommends use of a blow dryer.

For product testing, perhaps the two inventors should contact the government of Saskatchewan. The Canadian province tried to sell 1,000 erect wooden penises, originally meant to demonstrate condoms in sex education classes.
CRIME DOESNT PAY
Crime brought mixed results to its perpetrators across the world.
A car thief in California was "fingered" when he identified his missing digit in a hospital. The family who owned the van he had stolen had slammed the door on his hand.

In Sri Lanka, a would-be rapist got more than he bargained for when his victim doused him in a chilli solution, sending him fleeing in agony. He spent several hours covered in water before police arrested him.

Cayman Islands police, meanwhile, searched for a prankster who managed to bring the government to a halt. He or she smeared cow itch, a plant that causes rashes and itching, on a leading politician's jacket, causing the legislature to close for a day.
But as 1997 dawns a special toast is perhaps due to a hapless burglar in Denmark. Attempting to rob a butcher's shop, he fell into a vat of indelible sausage dye.
Police were searching for the -- literally -- red-faced perpetrator.
